---
title: "One end is all you need"
---

The generics part left you with a promise at the end of @sec-undo-generic: the
array inside `UndoStack<T>` would go, hand-built nodes would take its place, and
every test you had written would stay green. This chapter keeps that promise.
Then it gives the structure its real name and builds a second app on it, where
one rule about where a caboose may sit costs a single line.

## Keep the promise {#sec-stacks-undo}

1. Open `homework/undo-counter` from the last part and run `npm test`:

   ```text
    Test Files  2 passed (2)
         Tests  13 passed (13)
   ```

   That number is what the rest of this section is measured against. Leave
   `src/undo-stack.test.ts` and `src/command.test.ts` closed from here on. They
   are the measuring stick, and a measuring stick you bend to fit measures
   nothing.

2. Open `src/undo-stack.ts` and type in the `Node<T>` from @sec-linked-list-node,
   above the class. Every app in this part is its own project, so every one of
   them gets its own copy, and this copy carries no `export` either.

3. Throw the array out of the class and put two fields where it was:

   ```ts
   export class UndoStack<T> {
     private head: Node<T> | null = null;
     private count = 0;
   ```

4. Rewrite `push`. It builds a node and hooks it in front of the old top. Then
   `head` moves onto the new node:

   ```ts
     push(item: T): void {
       const node = new Node(item);
       node.next = this.head;
       this.head = node;
       this.count++;
     }
   ```

   The order of the middle two lines is not free. `node.next = this.head` has to
   run while `this.head` still holds the old top, because the line under it is
   the one that forgets the old top.

5. Rewrite `pop`. It answers `undefined` on an empty stack, and otherwise it
   hands the head's value back and moves `head` one step on:

   ```ts
     pop(): T | undefined {
       if (this.head === null) {
         return undefined;
       }

       const top = this.head;
       this.head = top.next;
       this.count--;
       return top.value;
     }
   ```

   Nothing deletes the old node. Once `head` stops pointing at it and `top` goes
   out of scope at the end of the method, nothing in your program can reach it,
   and the browser cleans it up on its own.

6. `clear` sets `head` back to `null` and `count` back to 0, which drops the
   whole chain in two lines. The `size` getter now returns `this.count` and stops
   asking an array.

7. Rewrite the `items` getter. It walks from the head to the end, collecting
   values as it goes, and turns the result around so the newest item is last:

   ```ts
     get items(): T[] {
       const result: T[] = [];
       let current = this.head;
       while (current !== null) {
         result.push(current.value);
         current = current.next;
       }

       result.reverse();
       return result;
     }
   ```

   `current` is the walker. It starts at the head, and `current = current.next`
   is the step that moves it along until it falls off the end into `null`.

8. Run `npm test` again:

   ```text
    Test Files  2 passed (2)
         Tests  13 passed (13)
   ```

Same number, and no test file was opened. Everything under the hood of
`UndoStack<T>` is different, and nothing that uses it noticed.

The one design decision worth arguing about is `count`. @sec-iteration-length
walked the chain for `length` instead of keeping a field, because a counter field
means every future method has to remember to update it. Here the price lands the
other way around. The counter app calls `render()` on every single click, and
`render()` reads `size` to decide whether the Undo button is gray. A walk would
count the whole history from scratch, every click, forever. The stack has four
methods that touch the chain and all four of them are on this screen, so keeping
`count` correct is a small job with a large payoff.

## The contract survives the rewrite {#sec-stacks-contract}

`UndoStack<T>.pop()` still says `T | undefined`, and that looks out of place in
this part. Everywhere else in Part 7, `null` is the answer to a question that came
back empty: `find` gives `Song | null`, and the queue in the next chapter gives
`T | null`. So why not tidy it up while you are in there?

Because the tests already say otherwise. Change that one word and the run comes
back like this:

```text
 FAIL  src/undo-stack.test.ts > UndoStack > gives back undefined when it is empty
AssertionError: expected null to be undefined

- Expected:
undefined

+ Received:
null
```

The return type of a public method is a promise the class made to everyone who
calls it, and the job today was to change the insides. Change the promise too and
every caller that tested for `undefined` is now asking the wrong question, while
the compiler can only warn about the callers it can see. Keep `undefined` here
and write `null` in the classes you start from scratch.

## What you just built is called a stack {#sec-stacks-lifo}

A **stack** is a collection where the item you take out is always the item you
put in most recently. The short name for that habit is **LIFO**, last in, first
out, and you have been using it all along: the last command you ran is the first
one Undo takes back.

Four methods cover almost everything a stack is asked to do.

* `push` puts an item on top
* `pop` takes the top item off and hands it back
* `peek` shows you the top item and leaves it there
* `isEmpty` says whether there is anything in it at all

A linked list needs a head pointer to start from, and it needs to walk when you
ask it to insert or delete somewhere in the middle. A stack never inserts in the
middle and never deletes in the middle. Both of its operations happen at the same
end. The head is that end, so a head pointer is the whole structure. That also
means `push` and `pop` cost the same tiny amount of work whether the stack holds
three items or three million, because neither of them ever looks past the first
node.

![Push hooks a new node in front of the head. Pop moves the head one step on and
hands the old head's value back. Neither one touches the rest of the
chain.](stack-push-pop.svg){width=460}

Stacks were already in your life before this chapter. The browser's Back button
pops the page you came from, which is why it takes you back one step at a time in
exactly the reverse order you arrived. Every error message you have ever read
prints a **call stack**: the function that threw sits at the top, the one that
called it is underneath, and reading down that list walks you back to where the
trouble started.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From last year's exam sheet

"This is only a warning. The cargo wagon **is** added, and the warning appears
only once."

Two details in that sentence decide where the check goes. *Is added* means the
warning cannot live in the branch that turns a part away, so it has to run after
the part is already on the train. *Only once* means the train has to remember
that it warned, which is one `boolean` field that starts at `false` and never
goes back.
:::

::: {.research title="Two questions the wiring asks"}
The exercise below hands you a page that builds its five buttons in a loop, and
it asks you to write a function that turns a string like `'cargo'` into a real
wagon object. Both lean on rules this chapter does not cover, and neither piece
of wiring will make sense until you have the answers.

1. The exercise asks you for a function `createPart(kind: PartKind)` built from a
   `switch` with one `case` per kind, no `default` clause, and a `return` in
   every case. TypeScript accepts that as a function that always gives back a
   `TrainPart`. What is that check called, and what does the compiler report the
   day somebody adds a sixth kind to `PartKind` and forgets the new `case`?
2. `src/index.ts` builds the five buttons with
   `for (const option of PART_OPTIONS)`, and each button gets its own `click`
   listener that reads `option`. When you click the cargo button, why does its
   listener see the cargo option instead of the caboose option that the loop
   ended on?

For the exam, question 2 has to be in your head. A listener written inside a loop
turns up in every second exercise, and the value it remembers is the part people
guess wrong.
:::

## Exercise: the train builder {#sec-stacks-exercise}

{{< exercise train-builder tests=true >}}

You assemble a train by coupling parts to its end, and you take parts off that
same end. That is a stack, so this app keeps its train in one, and the rules
about what may go where turn out to be questions the stack can already answer.

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `train-builder`. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`; the files
   you copy in bring their own `src/index.ts`.

2. Build the stack test-first in `src/stack.test.ts` and `src/stack.ts`, one
   sentence at a time as in @sec-undo-test-first. The class is
   `export class Stack<T>` with a private `head` and a `Node<T>` typed in above
   it, and these five members:

   ```ts
     push(item: T): void
     pop(): T | null
     peek(): T | null
     isEmpty(): boolean
     toArray(): T[]      // newest item first
   ```

   Nine sentences to write and make true:

   * a fresh stack is empty
   * it is not empty after one push
   * three pushed items come back newest first
   * it is empty again once everything has been popped
   * `pop()` on an empty stack gives `null`
   * `peek()` gives the newest item twice in a row and removes nothing
   * `peek()` on an empty stack gives `null`
   * `toArray()` lists two pushed items with the newest first
   * a `Stack<number>` holds numbers just as well as a `Stack<string>` holds
     strings

   This `pop` gives `null` where `UndoStack.pop()` gave `undefined`. Nothing has
   changed its mind: `UndoStack` kept `undefined` because its tests were written
   first and pinned it, while `Stack` is new today and follows the habit of this
   part.

3. Open `src/train-part.ts`. The union literal types and the abstract
   `TrainPart` are already there, and the five parts under the TODO comment are
   yours. Each one names its `kind` and its `restriction` as `readonly` fields
   and turns its constructor value into `detail`:

   ```ts
   export class Locomotive extends TrainPart {
     readonly kind: PartKind = 'locomotive';
     readonly restriction: PartRestriction = 'must-be-first';

     constructor(private readonly powerKw: number) {
       super();
     }

     get detail(): string {
       return `${this.powerKw} kW`;
     }
   }
   ```

   `PassengerWagon` (48 seats), `DiningWagon` (8 tables), and `Caboose` (2 crew)
   follow that shape with `'none'`, `'none'`, and `'must-be-last'`.
   `CargoWagon` (70 t max) is the one with something extra: it replaces the
   `cargoWeightTons` getter it inherited so that it reports its own weight
   instead of 0.

   Then write `createPart(kind: PartKind): TrainPart` at the bottom of the file,
   using the answer to the first research question. It is a **factory function**,
   which is the name for a function whose whole job is deciding which object to
   build for you.

4. Write `src/train.ts` test-first. `Train` keeps a `Stack<TrainPart>` and a
   `boolean` that remembers whether the heavy-cargo warning has been shown:

   ```ts
     add(part: TrainPart): string | null   // the message to show, or null
     removeLast(): void
     isEmpty(): boolean
     toArray(): TrainPart[]                // newest part first
   ```

   `add` is where the app lives. It starts with one `peek()`, which answers two
   questions at the same time: `null` means the train is empty, and a part means
   here is what a new part would be coupled behind. Then it decides in this
   order.

   * The train is empty and the part is not a `'must-be-first'` part: give back
     `'You need to place a locomotive first!'` and add nothing.
   * The train is not empty and the part is a `'must-be-first'` part: give back
     `'A train can only have one locomotive!'` and add nothing.
   * The part on top is a `'must-be-last'` part: give back
     `'The caboose must stay at the end of the train!'` and add nothing.
   * Otherwise push the part. Then add up `cargoWeightTons` over `toArray()`, and
     if the total is above 100 and no warning has been shown yet, remember that
     it has and give back
     `'Warning: this train is carrying a lot of cargo!'`.
   * Nothing to say: give back `null`.

   Notice what the third rule cost. The caboose rule sounds like a rule about the
   shape of the whole train, and it is one `peek` at a single node, because the
   only place a new part can land is the place `peek` shows you.

   Six sentences for `src/train.test.ts`:

   * a passenger wagon on an empty train is refused with the locomotive message,
     and the train stays empty
   * a locomotive on an empty train is accepted with no message
   * a second locomotive is refused with the one-locomotive message
   * a wagon behind a caboose is refused with the caboose message
   * behind a locomotive, the second cargo wagon of 70 tons brings the warning,
     a third one says nothing, and all four parts are on the train
   * `removeLast` after locomotive, passenger wagon, and caboose leaves two
     parts, and a passenger wagon is welcome again

5. Wire the page in `src/index.ts`, replacing the TODO comments. `src/styles.css`
   is already written and expects exactly this markup, so match the class names:

   * `showMessage(message: string | null)` puts the text into the message
     paragraph, and clears it for `null`
   * `render()` empties the train element with `replaceChildren()`. While the
     train is empty it appends one `<p class="hint">` reading
     `No train yet. Start with a locomotive.` For each part it appends a
     `<div>` carrying the classes `part` and the part's `kind`, holding a
     `<span class="part-kind">` with the kind and a `<span class="part-detail">`
     with the detail. Last, it disables the Remove-last button while the train is
     empty.
   * `toArray()` gives you the newest part first, and the locomotive belongs on
     the left, so `render()` draws the parts the other way around
   * the click listener of each part button builds the part for `option.kind`,
     offers it to the train, shows the message that comes back, and redraws
   * the Remove-last listener drops the newest part, clears the message, and
     redraws
   * `render()` runs once at the bottom of the file, so the fresh page shows its
     empty state and a gray Remove-last button

6. Run `npm start` and work through it. Expected results:

   * the empty page shows the hint and a gray Remove-last button
   * a passenger wagon first: the locomotive message appears and the train stays
     empty
   * a locomotive: it appears on the left, the message clears, and Remove-last
     wakes up
   * a second locomotive: the one-locomotive message, and the train still has one
     part
   * three cargo wagons in a row: the second one brings the heavy-cargo warning,
     and the third one says nothing
   * a caboose, then a dining wagon: the caboose message, and the dining wagon
     never appears
   * Remove-last: the caboose goes, the message clears, and a dining wagon is
     accepted now

7. Run `npm test` and expect `Tests  15 passed (15)`. Add the `verify` script
   with its three checks to `package.json` as in every new app, run
   `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Undo the removal.** Keep a second `Stack<TrainPart>` next to the train. Every
part that Remove-last takes off goes onto it, and a Put-back button pops from
there and offers the part to the train again. Adding a fresh part clears the
second stack, because the train just took a different turn. That is the same
shape as the redo stack of the counter app, built on the class you wrote today.

**A weight the user picks.** Give the cargo button a number input next to it and
build the `CargoWagon` from what the user typed, refusing anything that is not a
whole number of at least 1. The heavy-cargo warning gets a lot more interesting
once the wagons stop weighing 70 tons each.
:::
